title: Plant the golden set
brief: You have no labelled data and one domain expert with a free afternoon. The stage, the traffic and the drift you can tolerate are unspecified. Decide where cases come from and how you keep them honest.

blocks.title: Where golden cases come from
blocks.intro: Most strong sets mix sources. Pick the first source by stage, then add the others as traffic and budget appear.

options.name: Expert hand-written
options.summary: A domain expert writes questions, expected answers and, for retrieval, the relevant chunks.
pros: Targets the cases the business cares about
cons: Expert time is the scarcest resource
Small sets carry the author's blind spots
options.bestWhen: The first 20 to 50 cases, drawn from real failures, or any high-stakes domain.
options.avoidWhen: You need hundreds of cases by next week.

options.name: Mined from production traces
options.summary: Pick real queries from logged traces, then label them.
cons: Needs privacy and retention rules before reuse
Moves with users, so scores across refreshes are not comparable
options.bestWhen: Traffic exists and you want the set to follow real use.
options.avoidWhen: You are pre-launch, or you need a frozen baseline.

options.name: Synthetic from prompt and documents
options.summary: Foundry data generation from an agent definition, an inline prompt or a reference file, as Simple QnA or multi-turn Simulation seed.
pros: Stable baseline that does not drift with traffic
cons: Mirrors the generating prompt and can look uniform
options.bestWhen: You are pre-launch, traffic is low, or you need a regression baseline.
options.avoidWhen: It is the only source, or nobody reviews the rows.

options.name: Public benchmark
options.summary: A published suite such as GAIA, SWE-bench Verified or tau-bench used as a sanity check.
cons: Saturates and can leak into training data
Does not cover your data or tools
options.bestWhen: You are choosing a base model or tracking field-level capability.
options.avoidWhen: It stands in for a test on your own data.

steps.title: Seed
steps.md: Write 20 to 50 cases from real failures. Large early effects need few samples.

steps.title: Generate
steps.md: Make a small synthetic batch from the agent definition and reference files. Review rows by hand, then scale.

steps.title: Label
steps.md: One accountable expert adds expected answers, relevant chunk ids and written critiques.

steps.title: Version
steps.md: Tag each dataset version and record how each row was made: hand, trace or synthetic.

steps.title: Split
steps.md: Separate regression, capability and held-out slices. Nobody tunes on the held-out slice.

steps.title: Refresh
steps.md: Add failing production traces. Regenerate synthetic rows and bump the version when instructions change.

blocks.title: One golden row that serves retrieval and answer metrics
blocks.caption: Illustrative row. The first three keys follow the field names RAGAS and the Foundry Document Retrieval evaluator read. `origin`, `slice` and `dataset_version` are your own bookkeeping, and the policy text is invented.

items.label: Starter set
items.note: Simple tasks drawn from real failures

items.label: SWE-bench Verified
items.note: Human-validated subset. The original SWE-bench has 2,294 problems from 12 Python repositories

items.symptom: A benchmark score is high and the product disappoints
items.cause: Public suites saturate, leak into training data and do not cover your data
items.fix: Keep a private, held-out slice built from your own failures. Use public suites for model selection only.

items.symptom: Synthetic cases all look alike and every system passes
items.fix: Generate a small batch, review rows by hand, steer difficulty with a prompt plus a reference file, and add trace-derived cases.

items.symptom: Scores jump after a prompt edit with no real behaviour change
items.cause: The synthetic set mirrors the old instructions
items.fix: Regenerate and version the set when instructions change materially, and rerun the baseline on both versions.

items.symptom: The gate passes, then production regresses
items.cause: The gate set doubled as the tuning set
items.fix: Keep a held-out slice nobody tunes on, and refresh it from new traces.

items.symptom: A leaderboard result cannot be reproduced
items.cause: The benchmark changed grading between versions
items.fix: Pin the benchmark version. Scores from before tau-bench v1.0.1 (July 2026) are not comparable on banking_knowledge tasks.

blocks.title: Benchmarks age
blocks.md: OpenAI reportedly stopped evaluating on SWE-bench Verified in February 2026. The reasons given were score saturation (the top score moved from 74.9% to 80.9% in six months) and an audit of 138 hard tasks in which 59.4% had flawed tests or problem statements, plus signs of training-data leakage. The primary page blocked automated fetch on 2026-10-13, so these numbers come from a secondary write-up [[r48]]. GAIA took the opposite approach and withholds the answers to 300 of its 466 questions [[r33]].

quiz.q: You launch in two weeks, have no production traces, and need a baseline that will not drift as users change behaviour. Which source should supply the first set?
options: Synthetic cases from the agent definition and reference files, reviewed by hand
Traces mined from production logs, labelled by a domain expert after the first week
A public benchmark score for the chosen base model
Thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings collected after launch
quiz.explain: Synthetic generation works before launch and gives a stable regression baseline that does not move with traffic [[r8]]. Production traces do not exist yet and would drift once they do. A public benchmark score describes the base model, not your data or tools. Ratings arrive after launch, are biased toward vocal users and are not labelled test cases.

quiz.q: A teammate plans to submit these illustrative job settings to generate a first dataset. Which problem matters most?
options: The job exceeds the 100,000-row limit that applies to batch evaluation runs and will be rejected outright
max_samples is outside the documented 1 to 1,000 range, and a first batch should be reviewable
Simple QnA cannot take an agent definition as its source, only an inline prompt or a file
Synthetic generation requires an uploaded reference file in every job
quiz.explain: Evaluation jobs accept max_samples from 1 through 1,000, and the guidance is to start small and review rows manually before scaling [[r8]]. The 100,000-row figure is a different limit, on batch evaluation runs [[r37]]. Simple QnA needs an agent or prompt source, so an agent definition is allowed, and the reference file is optional.

quiz.q: Match each golden-set source to its defining trade-off.

pairs.r: Highest label quality, scarcest expert time
Follows real users but needs privacy rules and moves over time
Stable baseline that must be regenerated when instructions change
Comparable across systems but can saturate or leak into training data

quiz.explain: Each source pays for its strength somewhere else. Expert labels cost scarce hours. Traces bring realism and privacy duties, and the set drifts with users. Synthetic rows give a stable baseline but mirror the prompt that made them. Public suites compare systems but saturate, as the reported SWE-bench Verified retirement and GAIA's withheld answers show.

quiz.q: Select the practices Foundry guidance gives for synthetic evaluation datasets.
options: Generate a small batch first and review the rows by hand before scaling
Mirror the instructions your production agent actually runs
Regenerate and version the dataset when the agent's instructions change materially
Generate the maximum rows first, because a strong generator makes review unnecessary
quiz.explain: The guidance lists all three: a small first batch with manual review, instructions that match production because drift weakens the signal, and regeneration with a new version when the prompt changes [[r8]]. The fourth option fails because generator strength does not remove the need to spot-check rows, and an unreviewed maximum batch hides uniform or off-topic cases.

takeaways: Start with 20 to 50 cases from real failures. Expert time, not volume, is the constraint.
Record how each row was made and which dataset version it belongs to.
Synthetic rows give a stable pre-launch baseline and traces give realism. Use both.
Keep a held-out slice nobody tunes on, and pin benchmark versions.
Public benchmarks help pick a base model. Your own set gates your releases.
